articles.title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
articles.summary: The agreement will allow young people between 18 and 31 year-olds to travel, work or study in the EU for up to three years.
articles.body:
The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.

Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.

A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.

The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.

UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.

Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.

Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.

Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.

There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.

The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge.

The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530.

There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.

The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.

In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.

Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime.

"So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."

One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.

A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000.

If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially.

British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year.

The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027.

The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.

The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU.

The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a £570m contribution to the scheme.

In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027".

Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."

Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why...are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants?

"Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"

Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.

The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.

Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.

He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".

articles.title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing migrant dinghy
articles.summary: A judge called the anti-migrant activist a “publicity seeker” who disrupted the work of rescue crews.
articles.body:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.

Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.

His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.

Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.

He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.

The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.

He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.

It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".

Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".

He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".

After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.

Joel Smith KC, prosecuting, said it was "more a matter of luck than judgement that serious consequences did not arise".

The dinghy was later destroyed by French authorities, meaning the value of the damage could not be proven.

Judge James Newton-Price KC said it was "not for me to make any judgement of the political cause," but that the attack was "intended to have an impact on a live audience".

Commenting on the Border Force, coastguard and RNLI crews, he said: "They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover."

Simon Pentol KC, defending, said the dinghy did not sink and made its way back to France without help.

The judge accepted that prison had caused hardship for Thomas's family, including his four children. He said the sentence would have been 20 months had he gone to trial, and his time on remand would count towards it.

A separate charge of failing to give police the PIN to his phone, which Thomas denied, was ordered to lie on his file.

He is due to stand trial at Westminster Magistrates' Court in June over separate alleged offences in Dover, which he denies.

articles.title: After earning $3.50 a week as a store clerk, Frank Woolworth got $300 in backing for a five-cent shop; his first store failed, but the chain later topped 1,100 stores
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring journey of Frank Woolworth, who turned $300 into a retail giant with over 2,100 stores, revolutionizing the five-and-dime industry.
articles.body: Long before Frank Woolworth opened his first shop, he had personally experienced shopping as a poor customer. Once, being mocked for carrying loose change while shopping with his brother, he learned a valuable lesson. This childhood memory would be infused into his eventual business, making inexpensive merchandise its selling point.Early struggles and a five-cent pioneerAccording to the Woolworth Museum, Woolworth was born on 13 April 1852 in Rodman, New York. He grew up on his parents’ farm, left school at sixteen and worked on the farm. A family friend named Daniel McNeil helped him find work in commerce.On 24 March 1873, Woolworth started an apprenticeship at Augsbury and Moore, a dry-goods store in Watertown. He worked without pay for three months in return for board and lodging. The apprenticeship lasted for six months, and he earned $3.50 a week from the fourth month, the Woolworth Museum noted. He struggled with customers but proved his mettle in delivery, organising stock and arranging displays.In 1877, Moore wanted to clear surplus goods and put Woolworth in charge of a display where every item cost only five cents. Woolworth covered it in red cloth and added a large price sign. Customers bought the stock, and the store was forced to procure more merchandise from its wholesaler. The result gave Woolworth an idea to consider; it was whether a shop built around one low price could be self-sustainable.False starts, Lancaster success and rapid expansionWoolworth’s first five-cent shop in Utica, New York, however, did not last. Undaunted by the failure, he next opened in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, on 21 June 1879, according to the Woolworth Museum. The tipping point had come with an offer from a former employer named William Moore, who advanced $300 worth of stock, the museum noted.The Lancaster store opened as the F.W. Woolworth Great Five-Cent Store. Its first day's takings were $127.65, according to the Woolworth Museum. Within a fortnight, Woolworth opened another branch in Harrisburg, managed by his brother Sumner. When the landlord sought higher rent, Sumner moved it to Reading, and the next stop was Scranton. Relatives and former colleagues helped establish five-and-ten-cent shops across North America.Woolworth organised independent chains into the Friendly Rival Syndicate. Members pitched ideas and bought common merchandise while retaining their own businesses. According to the Library of Congress, in February 1905, F.W. Woolworth & Company was formally incorporated. Employees and friends were allowed to buy shares, although the stock was not put up for public sale. In 1912, Woolworth and five other retailers merged their businesses and brought together 596 stores across 37 states under the company, the Library of Congress noted.Going global and wartime pivotsWoolworth established a British subsidiary in 1909 and appointed his second cousin, Fred Moore Woolworth, in charge, the Library of Congress noted. The first shop in Britain opened on Church Street in Liverpool. The management team included experienced employees and William Lawrence Stephenson, who had worked for a British supplier.The British business prospered quickly. The Library of Congress records 44 stores in the British Isles by 1914. The company’s headquarters in New York, the Woolworth Building, was completed in 1913. It stood over 792 feet tall and remained the world’s tallest building until 1929, the Library of Congress noted. The chain continued to expand in 1924 and 1926 when the company opened up in Cuba and Germany.During the First World War, European supplies had become difficult to obtain. Imported goods represented a quarter of Woolworth’s sales and a larger share of its profits. Drawing from his experience of factory visits in Europe, Woolworth encouraged American manufacturers to produce goods domestically. By 1915, US sources had been established for all previously imported items, the Woolworth Museum noted.End of an eraWoolworth passed away on 8 April 1919 after four decades of leading the company. The Woolworth Museum recorded 1,100 stores in the chain at his death, with outlets in the United States, Canada, Ireland and Great Britain. The Library of Congress traced the later corporate changes: the company came to be known as Venator Group in 1998. In 2001, it disposed of its non-athletic business and took the name Foot Locker, Inc.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Watch: Paper bombs hurled, firecrackers bursted outside education ministry in Italy as protests intensify
articles.summary: A student protest in Rome turned confrontational on Friday, as demonstrators hurled paper bombs, bottles and firecrackers at the ministry of education
articles.body: A student protest in Rome turned confrontational on Friday, as demonstrators hurled paper bombs, bottles and firecrackers at the ministry of education amid a nationwide strike and student mobilisation across Italy.Protesters also threw a road sign and an electric scooter at the building as police were deployed to protect the ministry, according to local media reports.Footage from outside the ministry showed two young men sitting on its steps as hooded protesters hurled paper bombs at officers deployed to guard the building. The demonstration coincided with a nationwide 24-hour strike called by the CGIL trade union, which triggered disruptions to transport, schools and other services.The strike saw demonstrations in more than 100 Italian cities, including Milan, Turin, Naples, Palermo and Rome. Protesters denounced stagnant wages, rising living costs and what organisers described as the government's failure to strengthen public services and worker protections.The labour action also coincided with an International Day of Student Mobilisation, with student groups organising demonstrations in more than 45 cities across Italy. They called for greater investment in education, measures to address the cost-of-living crisis and policies aimed at reducing inequality.Protests spread across EuropeThe demonstrations in Italy were part of a wider wave of labour and student protests across Europe, with rallies also held in Croatia, Austria and Germany over education funding, housing, public services and military spending.In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.Meanwhile, demonstrators in Germany called for greater education funding and opposed a possible return to compulsory military service. The rallies came weeks after protests on October 31 that drew thousands into the streets and saw violent incidents in some cities.Strike disrupts services in ItalyThe strike in Italy covered both the public and private sectors, with public transport services reduced or disrupted in several cities. Schools and some health facilities were also affected.Planned strikes by air transport workers were cancelled for Friday, though separate walkouts involving airport personnel remain scheduled for Sunday at Milan and Venice airports.Authorities deployed additional police in several Italian cities where multiple demonstrations took place. Alongside the CGIL action, grassroots unions including Cobas organised separate strikes and marches, adding to the scale of the nationwide mobilisation.The protests also took on a political dimension, with opposition leaders joining demonstrations and criticising Premier Giorgia Meloni's government over wages and social spending.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'What happens in GTA 6 stays in GTA 6': Police across US warn fans about taking the game to their real lives
articles.summary: The game's fans waited over a decade for this moment, and now police are reminding them "real-life laws don't come with cheat codes, respawns, or mission restarts".
articles.body:
Police departments are reminding Americans that street racing, auto theft and gun violence are still crimes in real life, as excitement over Grand Theft Auto 6, a game following the lives of career criminals, reaches a fever pitch in the US.

"Play the game. Don't play yourself," Atlanta police warned in a social media post, while Denver authorities said that "running from police is still illegal".

Over 20 million units of the game have been purchased worldwide since its release this week, making GTA 6 likely the biggest entertainment launch in history.

The game, known for its freedom of play, ranging from buying a cheeseburger to firing a grenade launcher, is set in a Florida-inspired state.

"Assaulting someone for extra points, it's not worth it," an officer from the San Antonio Police Department, in Texas, said in a video.

Since Rockstar Games' 1997 inaugural release in the Grand Theft Auto series, the game has been both celebrated and condemned for its depictions of violence and its invitation to players to virtually participate.

It allows players to do everything from selling drugs to soliciting prostitutes and shooting law enforcement officers.

GTA 6's release in the US on Thursday ended a 13-year break in the series, unleashing a surge of fan enthusiasm and also concern among police departments.

"We need to talk," the San Juan Police Department, also in Texas, said in a video published on Instagram the same day the game launched in the US.

"We know you're excited and we know you've been waiting a long time, but what happens in GTA 6 stays in GTA 6."

In Arizona, the Pima County Sheriff's Office told GTA 6 fans in a Facebook post: "Real-life laws don't come with cheat codes, respawns, or mission restarts."

Law enforcement officials weren't the only ones worried, with one pundit on Fox News wondering if the game might "destigmatise crime". Rosanna Scotto also raised the question of whether it made young people "more inclined to use guns at an earlier age now because of these kind of video games".

Research on the relationship between video game violence and its effects on players is mixed.

The American Psychological Association (APA) issued a resolution in 2020 that said "violence is a complex social problem that likely stems from many factors".

"Attributing violence to violent video gaming is not scientifically sound and draws attention away from other factors," the APA said.

But the APA also said research showed an association between violent video games and increased aggressive behaviour and decreased moral judgement.

Despite concerns, the release of GTA 6 has had a meteoric landing , topping $2.36bn (£1.8bn) in first-day sales, and generating news headlines over the surge in people skipping school and work in order to play.

articles.title: Two men dead after glider crashes into Loch Leven
articles.summary: The Scottish Gliding Centre said a two-seater Perkoz aircraft had "crashed whilst on a local training flight".
articles.body:
Two men have died after a glider crashed into Loch Leven.

Police, ambulance, fire service and the coastguard were called to the scene near Kinross at about 11:00.

The Scottish Gliding Centre, which is based at Portmoak Airfield near the loch, said a two-seater Perkoz aircraft had "crashed whilst on a local training flight" but it was not clear what had caused the crash.

Police Scotland said the deaths were not being treated as suspicious and inquiries were ongoing to establish the full circumstances.

The Scottish Gliding Centre spokesperson added: "The incident is currently under investigation by the Air Accidents Investigation Branch of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.

"Our club is co-operating fully with these organisations."

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it had launched an investigation and sent a team of inspectors to the accident site.

Local airspace restrictions remain in place.

An AAIB spokesperson said: "A multi-disciplinary team including inspectors with expertise in aircraft operations, engineering and recorded data have been deployed to gather evidence and make inquiries."

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said operations mobilised one fire engine and specialist resources to the area to assist emergency service partners.

The spokesperson said fire crews had since left the scene.

Two HM Coastguard helicopters and an air ambulance also joined the emergency response.

articles.title: Nikhil Gupta gets nearly 20 years in US jail for plot to kill Khalistani separatist Pannun
articles.summary: Indian national, Nikhil Gupta, was sentenced to 235 months (nearly 19 years and seven months) in prison by a US federal court on Friday for his role in a
articles.body: Indian national, Nikhil Gupta, was sentenced to 235 months (nearly 19 years and seven months) in prison by a US federal court on Friday for his role in a murder-for-hire plot targeting Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. US District Judge Victor Marrero announced the sentence in the Southern District of New York. Pannun, who holds American and Canadian citizenship, was present in court when the verdict was pronounced.Gupta, 55, had pleaded guilty earlier this year to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The plot involved attempts to hire a hitman to kill Pannun on American soil.The sentence of 235 months is at the lower end of the US Sentencing Guidelines range of 235 to 293 months. Last week, the US government had sought a 293-month prison term, arguing that Gupta's actions warranted a severe punishment.In a 20-page submission to the court, US Attorney James McDonald described Gupta's conduct as "as brutal as it was brazen"."He was a crucial participant in a foreign plot to execute a US citizen on US soil. The Court should impose a sentence that reflects the magnitude of the crime and sends a message that the violent silencing of voices in this country will not be tolerated," McDonald said.The US government alleged that Gupta and his co-conspirators, including at least one Indian government employee, plotted to kill an American citizen because of the "victim's political ideology"."It is a crime of the utmost seriousness and demands an equally serious penalty…. the Government submits that a sentence at the top of the United States Sentencing Guidelines range of 235 to 293 months’ incarceration is necessary to serve the legitimate purposes of sentencing," the submission said.What Gupta's lawyers arguedGupta's lawyers had sought a substantially reduced sentence of 144 months, followed by three years of supervised release. They backed the Probation Department's recommendation for a downward variance from the sentencing guidelines.His defence argued that Gupta had no previous criminal record and was suffering from untreated alcohol dependence at the time of the offence. They also said that a lengthy prison term would carry significant consequences for the 55-year-old."Gupta does not minimise" the seriousness of his actions, his lawyers told the court. They acknowledged that he had agreed to arrange a murder but argued that the punishment should be proportionate."He agreed to arrange the murder of another person, and that conduct warrants a term of imprisonment. But the sentence this Court imposes should be sufficient, and not greater than necessary, to serve the purposes of sentencing as to this defendant," his lawyers said.Gupta expressed regret in letter to courtIn a letter submitted to the court, Gupta said he wished he could "turn back time to 2023 and undo my mistakes".He added that when he looked back at his actions, "I don’t even recognise the man I had become."Gupta said he had become distant from his family in early 2023 and started drinking heavily almost every night. He also expressed regret over the suffering caused to his family and others."I deeply regretted the suffering I caused them and the people around me," he wrote.He also told the court that he was "so thankful that my actions did not result in the loss of human life or injury", adding that such an outcome "would have been the greatest regret of my life."How the murder plot unfoldedAccording to the indictment, other public court documents and statements made in court, Gupta worked with associates in India and elsewhere in 2023 to plan Pannun's assassination in the US.The alleged plot involved co-defendant Vikash Yadav, whom US prosecutors identified as an Indian government employee.At Yadav's direction, Gupta contacted a person he believed was a criminal associate to arrange a hitman to kill Pannun in New York City. However, the person was actually a confidential source working with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).Yadav subsequently agreed, through arrangements brokered by Gupta, to pay the undercover source $100,000 to carry out the killing.On or around June 9, 2023, Gupta and Yadav arranged for an associate to deliver $15,000 in cash to the undercover source as an advance payment for the planned murder.You use AI every day. articles.title: Man jailed for murder of Jennifer Symonds in River Thames at Henley
articles.summary: Nelio Gouveia, 45, is jailed for killing Jennifer Symonds, who drowned in the River Thames.
articles.body:
A man has been jailed for life with a minimum of 22 years and six months after he murdered a woman, who was found drowned in the River Thames, while serving a suspended prison sentence.

The body of Jennifer Symonds, 44, was recovered from the river at Phyllis Court Club in Henley-on-Thames on the morning of 6 March 2026.

Last month, Nelio Gouveia, 45, of Phyllis Court Drive, Henley-on-Thames, pleaded guilty to her murder during an appearance at Oxford Crown Court .

During a hearing at the same court on Friday, Gouveia was handed the mandatory life sentence for murder and ordered to serve at least 22 years and six months behind bars.

It can now also be reported that Gouveia had been serving a two-year suspended prison sentence for a violent attack on a woman at the time of the murder.

Jailing him on Friday, Judge Jay said Gouveia's actions "stemmed from your propensity in certain circumstances to violence against women".

Reacting to the sentence, Gouveia, who appeared in the dock wearing a grey tracksuit and clutching white rosary beads, looked down at the floor.

His defence had earlier told the hearing that "he doesn't feel he is worthy of forgiveness and is deeply remorseful of what he has done".

Friday's hearing was told that Gouveia and Symonds had likely met on Red Lion Lawn in Henley and had been exchanging infrequent text messages.

On 5 March, the pair agreed to meet up at the theatre in the town, before spending the night together.

Gouveia then left Symonds at a pavilion by the water at Phyllis Court in the early hours, before he returned with a metal weight lifting dumbbell and attacked her.

CCTV of the attack was not played in court, with the judge describing it as "deeply disturbing and upsetting".

Thames Valley Police launched a murder investigation after being called to Phyllis Court Drive at about 07:50 GMT on 6 March.

Gouveia was arrested the same day, and charged on 8 March. A post-mortem examination showed Symonds had died from drowning.

Portugal-born Gouveia worked and lived as a kitchen porter at the Phyllis Court private members' club on the banks of the River Thames.

The court heard a fellow employee at the members' club had reported that Gouveia said: "If girls are annoying and aren't behaving, you just hit them."

The 45-year-old was sentenced in 2024 to a two year suspended prison sentence for assault occasioning actual bodily harm after he punched a woman in the face in 2022.

Gouveia also poured red wine over the victim, before hitting her over the head with a bottle.

"I genuinely believed that he was going to kill me or cause me some serious harm," the victim said afterwards.

Symonds was born in Zambia and moved to the UK aged three. She had worked for Microsoft until being made redundant in 2025.

Before her death, the court was told she had been seeking to rejoin the army cadets as a volunteer.

At Friday's hearing, Symonds' older brother Andrew emotionally described her as "vivacious" and "outgoing" with a "quiet sense of rebellion wrapped in imagination and warmth".

In a statement read out by the prosecution, her parents said she had been "loving kind, generous and caring" and "touched so many lives in a really positive way".

"She was an integral part of our lives. The grief and trauma is devastating," they added.

The court was also told that Symonds had pursued many outdoor activities and enjoyed being out in nature and by the river in Henley.

Her friend, Gary Hamilton, told the BBC ahead of the hearing that she loved spending time on his boat, and would "try any new adventure".

"Her laugh was very infectious", he said. "She was really, very, very bubbly."

"She'd always be looking out for people. So if anybody was wanting a conversation or down or anything, I know she'd go to them."

"The whole community has been mourning for her."

Symonds' friend Cameron Finlay-Cooper, 32, described the moment he found out about her death as a "sucker punch".

"It's just abhorrently awful, there's no other word to describe it. It really is just a wound that a lot of people are trying to recover from," he told the BBC.

"She really was loved by everyone in this town," he said, adding that his friend would be remembered for being a "really incredible person".

Jonathan Barter wants to install a memorial to his friend near to her favourite spot along the River Thames.

"It just occurred to me that perhaps the town council would consider allowing us to put a plaque in her memory."

Suggesting the Red Lion Lawn in Henley as its location, he said: "She lived just up the road here.. and I think was really her quiet place."

"I thought we mustn't let Jen be forgotten."

articles.title: Dwain Hall found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby
articles.summary: Dwain Hall has been found guilty of the kidnap and first-degree murder of Sonia Exelby.
articles.body:
A man has been found guilty of the kidnap and murder of a woman who he groomed on a fetish website.

Dwain Hall, 54, convinced 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Southsea, Hampshire, to travel to the United States where he stabbed her to death.

On Friday he was found guilty following a trial at a court in Ocala, Florida, of kidnap and first-degree murder. He was then sentenced to life in prison.

Exelby's body was found buried in Marion County, Florida, on 17 October 2025 after she was reported missing from her home five days earlier.

The trial of Hall, whose online username was Alpha Sadist, was told he had been the "executioner" of Sonia Exelby and had demanded she pay $4,000 (£3,000) for him to kill her.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

Hall was impassive as the unanimous verdict of the Florida jury was read out.

The court in Florida heard that the 32-year-old, who had struggled with mental illness, had wanted to die.

Assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said on the first day of the trial on Tuesday that Sonia Exelby met the defendant on a now-defunct website and "he manipulated her for years".

"He targeted her because of her mental illness and he exploited her for his own sadistic pleasure," she said.

"And when he finally got her alone, thousands of miles away from home, completely incapable of making any rational decisions, he stabbed her to death and buried her body."

Berndt said Exelby had been "trying to find someone who would kill her," adding: "Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible."

Sonia Exelby's sister, Gemma Isaj, who gave evidence during the trial, said following the guilty verdict: "A vulnerable person was preyed upon. A beautiful soul was taken.

"Our lives will never be the same again. We must learn a new way of being.

"When this tragedy began to unfold, Sonia really believed that she could stop others from getting hurt. And I believe that today's justice has done that.

"Furthermore, she shone the spotlight on the darkness of such sites, like Motherless.com.

"In some capacity, we will continue to fight for mental health in her name."

Her brother, Barry Wilton, said: "I know Sonia would be so distraught to see the aftermath of her death.

"Dwain, you pretended to care for Sonia. You didn't at all. You used her to fulfil your sick fantasies.

"You had her life in your hands. You had the opportunity to save her, but instead you preyed on her vulnerabilities and you took her from us."

Sonia Exelby was reported missing from her home on 12 October last year, by which time police established she had left the country.

After her body was found by US investigators Hall was traced by police through the attempted use of the victim's credit card by the roadside assistance company he owned.

Earlier, the jury heard that Exelby's consent was not a defence to the crime of first-degree murder.

They were also told consent meant intelligent, knowing, voluntary consent, and did not include coerced submission, through the use of exploitation, threats of force, or intimidation.

articles.title: Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
articles.summary: Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating.
articles.body:
Protesters have rallied across 25 European countries amid a wave of public discontent over issues ranging from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people.

Inspired by demonstrations that have shaken France in recent months, thousands took to the streets in countries including the United Kingdom, Austria, Germany, Spain, Italy, Sweden and Croatia on Friday.

Tens of thousands of workers and students protested in more than 100 Italian cities to demand higher wages ⁠⁠and greater investment in public services.

The rallies coincided with a general strike by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL, that involved workers in ‌‌both the private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare.

“Across Europe and among ordinary people, the demand for change is growing,” CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said at a rally in Rome.

Demonstrators in Rome threw objects at the Ministry of Education, while in Bologna some protesters clashed with police, news agency ANSA reported. In Milan, demonstrators set fire to a cardboard tanker as well as cardboard figures depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and United States President Donald Trump.

The Italian rallies ⁠⁠followed a nationwide mobilisation on October 17 that descended into rioting and looting and prompted the right-wing government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to approve sweeping security measures and deploy the army alongside police in subsequent demonstrations.

Student groups have since continued protests and occupations at schools and universities, with opposition to higher military spending also emerging as a rallying cry.

Opposition leaders joining demonstrations on Friday criticised Meloni’s government and its budget policies amid rising living costs. Elly Schlein, leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, said the 2027 Budget Law “does not have a vision for the future of the country” as it does not help industries but slashes funding for public healthcare and education.

Meanwhile, in Germany, campaign group “Gen Z regelt” (German for “Gen Z sorts it”) said it ⁠⁠was organising protests in 73 cities and towns.

In Berlin, roughly 4,000 people attended a protest in the city’s ⁠⁠Alexanderplatz square.

The Cologne protest drew fewer than the 5,000 people expected, though ⁠⁠demonstrators still numbered in the thousands, police said.

Protesters gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service.

In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.

In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.

Demonstrations across Europe were inspired by much larger protests in France that began in September and descended into violent confrontations with the police and looting.

On Tuesday, France’s Interior Ministry said a total of 146,000 people took part in protests across the country , with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.

The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency.

Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 percent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 percent in Spain, 11 percent in France and 20 percent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.

articles.title: ‘Our nation has a mass incarceration problem’: Mamdani sets 2032 deadline to close notorious Rikers Island jail
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a plan to shut down the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, five years beyond the original
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a plan to shut down the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, five years beyond the original deadline, with the strategy depending on reducing the number of people held in custody and shifting inmates to smaller facilities across the city.According to the Associated Press, Mamdani unveiled the plan on Friday, saying the extended timeline was necessary after delays under the previous administration. The city had been legally required to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller jails by 2027, a target it is now almost certain to miss.“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” Mamdani said, describing the jail as a place the city had avoided confronting for decades.“Our nation has a very real mass incarceration problem,” he said. “We are making a conscious decision to advance a new model of a criminal legal system in our city, one that takes on that problem head on.”Plan focuses on reducing jail populationThe Mamdani administration aims to bring down the number of people held at Rikers from around 6,700 currently to slightly more than 4,000.The proposed measures include expanding diversion and supervised-release programmes, increasing access to housing and social services, restoring an online bail payment system and reducing delays in court proceedings. The administration says these steps would help prevent repeat offences and reduce the time people spend behind bars.The mayor also said the city needed a different approach to its criminal justice system, arguing that the US faced a serious problem of mass incarceration.Under the plan, inmates would gradually be moved from Rikers, an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport, to smaller jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan. Some people requiring medical or psychiatric care would be transferred to specialised facilities.The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women and expand community-based alternatives.Four borough jails to replace RikersAccording to the timeline announced by City Hall, the new Brooklyn jail is expected to open in 2029, followed by facilities in the Bronx and Queens in 2031.The Manhattan jail is scheduled to open in 2032. The revised deadlines will require approval from the New York City Council.Rikers has faced years of criticism over violence, overcrowding and poor conditions. A federal judge previously described conditions at the complex as “abnormal and unacceptable” and appointed an outside manager to oversee reforms.The City Council voted in 2019 to close the facility and replace it with four smaller jails by 2027. However, the plan faced political resistance, including from former mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and the borough jail proposal.Mamdani said his administration was determined to complete the closure after decades of delays. City Council Speaker Julie Menin also backed the revised plan, saying the city was finally getting the project back on track.

articles.title: Andy Burnham: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal
articles.summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others

articles.title: Two deals done, 10 more in pipeline: Trump's trade promise after Asia trip
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday said the United States expects to secure about 10 more trade deals soon, following his four-day trip to Asia, during
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Friday said the United States expects to secure about 10 more trade deals soon, following his four-day trip to Asia, during which he met more than 20 world leaders, including the presidents of China and Russia.Recounting the trade discussions at a White House news conference, Trump said the US had already secured two new trade deals, with about 10 others expected to follow.“In four days, I met more than 20 world leaders, secured two new trade deals — and about 10 others coming very soon — attended four major international summits, reaffirmed America’s alliances throughout the region and advanced the cause of peace and security around the world,” he said.“The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength,” Trump added.The president also addressed the US energy market, linking domestic petrol prices to the outcome of Washington's engagement with Iran. His comments come amid continuing tensions between the two countries and efforts to address their differences."Gas prices depend on how we settle with Iran," Trump said. He also indicated that Tehran was interested in reaching an agreement. "They want a deal," he said.Trump renews criticism of Federal ReserveThe US president also criticised the Federal Reserve's monetary policy, arguing that interest rates remained too high. He blamed what he described as a politically influenced central bank for the situation."Interest rates too high because we have political Fed," Trump said.Trump has repeatedly called for lower borrowing costs, arguing that cheaper credit would benefit the US economy. However, the Federal Reserve sets interest rates independently through its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which considers factors including inflation, employment and economic activity.The president said the United States should have the lowest borrowing costs globally."We should have lowest interest rate in world," he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Denver police detective accused of drunk driving, hitting parked car and fleeing in city-provided SUV; deputies stop her at gunpoint, later identify her as 26-year veteran Jamie Major
articles.summary: A 61-year-old Denver police detective is facing charges after allegedly driving under the influence, crashing an unmarked police SUV into a parked car and
articles.body: A 61-year-old Denver police detective is facing charges after allegedly driving under the influence, crashing an unmarked police SUV into a parked car and fleeing the scene in an Arapahoe County neighbourhood. The incident, which took place on August 28, took a dramatic turn when deputies eventually stopped the damaged vehicle and pulled the driver out at gunpoint, according to reports cited by CBS Colorado.The driver was identified as Jamie Major, a 26-year veteran of the Denver Police Department. She was behind the wheel of a 2024 Chevrolet Tahoe provided by the City of Denver for her use. The unmarked SUV was fitted with a police radio, a department safety vest and a light bar.SUV allegedly flees after crashing into parked carThe incident occurred at around 10.30 pm in the Holly Hills neighbourhood. According to reports from the Arapahoe County Sheriff's Office and Colorado State Patrol, the Tahoe struck a parked car before driving away.The impact was loud enough to bring several neighbours outside. A nearby Ring camera also captured footage of the SUV leaving the scene, CBS Colorado reported.One resident, who requested anonymity, said people rushed out after hearing a noise that sounded like a dumpster being dropped."Very quickly after the collision, you could see the car pull away and attempt to leave the scene, and everyone was a witness to that," she told the news outlet.Her husband, an Army veteran, then got into his vehicle and followed the SUV, hoping to help prevent it from putting other motorists and residents at risk.The Tahoe had reportedly lost its right front tyre in the collision. Despite the damage, it continued moving on one rim and travelled around a mile before deputies caught up with it near Yale and Monaco.Deputies use 'pinch' manoeuvre to stop vehicleAccording to the reports, deputies used a "pinch" manoeuvre to block the SUV and bring it to a stop. They described the vehicle as presenting a danger to everyone on the road.Deputies initially believed the SUV could have been stolen. They pulled the driver out at gunpoint and subsequently identified her as Major.The sheriff's report stated that Major smelled of alcohol and appeared to have difficulty standing. Deputies also reported finding a full bottle of alcohol inside the vehicle.One deputy described the driver's conduct as "egregious" and cited her alleged unwillingness to stop. The report said the deputy and another officer drew their service weapons and pointed them at the driver as a show of force.Major was not wearing her police uniform and was reportedly wearing only one sandal when she stepped out of the SUV. She then told deputies that she was a Denver Police detective.Major faces multiple charges and resigns from police departmentMajor was charged with driving under the influence, leaving the scene of an accident, failing to report an accident and careless driving.Following the incident, the Denver Police Department demoted her. She resigned from the department on November 2, while its internal investigation was still underway, according to officials.Her attorney, William Khoury Dillon, declined to comment on the allegations in detail."We don't want to try this matter in the media. We are looking forward to this process playing out in the criminal justice system," he said.The Colorado State Patrol, which is the primary agency investigating the incident, declined to release any video related to the case, citing the ongoing investigation.The Denver Department of Public Safety also declined to share photographs of the damaged police SUV with CBS Colorado. The department said the Tahoe had been repaired and returned to service.Brent Weisberg, director of marketing and communications for the department, said officials would not comment while the criminal and internal proceedings were pending."As the criminal and internal cases are pending, neither the Department of Public Safety nor the Denver Police Department will comment on the allegations," he said.Neighbours raise concerns over accountabilityThe incident has prompted questions among residents about how a serving police detective could allegedly be involved in a hit-and-run while driving a city-provided vehicle. Neighbours have also questioned why civilians had to follow the SUV after the collision.The woman who witnessed the incident said her husband was particularly upset after learning that the driver was a police officer and that the vehicle was paid for by taxpayers.Another resident, whose parked car was reportedly totalled in the crash, said she was surprised that the driver did not stop to leave a note or inform her about the damage. She also requested that her identity not be disclosed.One neighbour said the case had reinforced her belief that law enforcement officials should be held to the same standards as everyone else."Nobody should be above the law, even the people enforcing it," she said.The criminal case against Major remains pending. articles.title: Jersey's and Guernsey's governments welcome new UK-EU deal
articles.summary: Jersey's and Guernsey's governments say the package will especially benefit trade and young people.
articles.body:
The Channels Islands are set to benefit from a new deal for a closer working relationship between the UK and European Union (EU), the islands' governments have said.

On Friday the UK and EU agreed a new deal covering food exports, youth mobility and carbon emissions.

Both Jersey's and Guernsey's governments said the new package would make trade easier as from March 2028 most checks on food, fish and agricultural goods moving between the UK, EU and Crown Dependencies are set to end.

It would also allow islanders aged 18 to 31 to live, work, volunteer and study in the EU for two years and Channel Islands students studying at UK higher education settings will be able to study in Europe.

The package also secures the return of pet passports, making travel between the islands and the EU easier for those with animals.

A specific exemption has been been secured with the EU to protect Guernsey and Jersey's dairy industries and the ban on importing cows will remain.

Policy and Resources Committee President Deputy Lindsay de Sausmarez said: "Although Brexit was a decision for the UK, it inadvertently had a big impact on us here in the bailiwick, too.

"It's taken a lot of time, effort and resources to manage the additional legislation and other local requirements brought about by Brexit, and it's also created a lot of extra red tape for islanders and businesses."

She said States would consider proposals early in the new year and, if agreed, "the benefits should start to be felt in 2028".

Jersey's External Relations Minister Senator Ian Gorst welcomed the announcement.

"Government officers have worked closely with the UK to make sure Jersey's interests were understood throughout the talks," he said.

"That important work has helped secure a strong outcome for our island and will now focus on making sure Jersey is ready for the changes from 2028."

articles.title: A Virginia city spent $22.5 million building a road near an Amazon fulfilment centre; after hundreds of complaints about truck traffic and speeding, councillors have voted to close part of it
articles.summary: Councillors in Virginia Beach have voted to permanently close part of a newly built $22.5 million road near a large Amazon fulfilment centre.
articles.body: Councillors in Virginia Beach have voted to permanently close part of a newly built $22.5 million road near a large Amazon fulfilment centre. The decision follows hundreds of complaints from residents about heavy lorry traffic, speeding and dangerous driving in nearby neighbourhoods. The road, known as the West Mall Drive extension, was completed in 2025 to improve access to the large e-commerce facility. However, soon after it opened, residents living nearby began reporting problems with commercial vehicles using the route. The road was originally designed mainly for passenger cars, not heavy lorries.At a meeting on Tuesday, 17 November 2026, the Virginia Beach City Council voted unanimously to close the section. City staff had recorded more than 100 complaints about speeding lorries, excessive noise and safety problems along the residential stretch, according to WHRO Public Media. "It was never the intention of the design to route significant heavy truck traffic through that corridor," Virginia Beach City Manager Patrick Duhaney told WHRO. "The primary purpose was to accommodate employee commuter traffic." Residents who had asked the council to take action welcomed the decision. Speaking at the meeting, local homeowner Sharon Miller said the situation had become unbearable. She described constant vibrations caused by passing lorries and near-miss accidents involving children. "We are talking about semi-trucks navigating what was supposed to be a neighbourhood connector road. The noise is deafening and we fear for our safety every single day," Miller told council members.Traffic study confirms heavy commercial vehicle useCity officials ordered a traffic study to check residents' complaints. The findings showed that large numbers of commercial vehicles, including heavy lorries travelling to the Amazon facility, were using the West Mall Drive extension instead of the designated truck routes. Engineers found that the road's layout and surface had not been designed to handle the regular weight and volume of large lorries. The study warned that the heavy traffic was wearing down the road faster than expected and creating dangerous conditions for pedestrians and cyclists. The study also found that many vehicles were travelling above the posted speed limit, with some drivers exceeding it by a considerable amount.Implementation of closure and future accessThe council's vote allows the city to close a specific section of West Mall Drive immediately. City workers are expected to put up concrete barriers and road signs within the coming weeks to stop vehicles from passing through. The closure will prevent drivers from travelling directly between the residential neighbourhood and the commercial areas around the Amazon fulfilment centre. Residents will still be able to reach their homes from one direction, but the road will no longer provide a continuous route through the area. City planners admitted that the change would make some journeys longer for commuters. However, they said the closure was necessary to improve safety and reduce disruption for local residents.Virginia Beach Mayor Bobby Dyer supported the decision, saying the safety and quality of life of residents were more important than keeping traffic moving through the area. "Our first and foremost obligation is to ensure the safety and well-being of our citizens," Dyer said during the council meeting. "We listened to the outcry from the community and we are taking decisive action to address it. We cannot allow neighbourhoods to be transformed into industrial thoroughfares."Amazon's position and alternative routesAmazon representatives did not attend Tuesday's public meeting. However, the company has previously said it is committed to working with local authorities on traffic management plans. Amazon officials have said that delivery drivers are instructed to use designated main truck routes, including nearby major roads. It remains unclear why so many commercial vehicles were using the West Mall Drive extension instead of following those routes. City officials said they would continue working with Amazon to make sure its navigation systems and delivery instructions direct drivers away from the residential section that is being closed.Closing the road represents a major financial loss for the city, which spent $22.5 million on the project just a year earlier. However, councillors decided that protecting public safety and residents' quality of life was more important than the money already spent on that section of the road. The remaining sections of West Mall Drive will stay open and continue serving the areas they were built to connect. City staff will now focus on installing permanent physical barriers to prevent vehicles from using the closed section.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Russia complains of ‘new Iron Curtain’ as Estonia shuts its borders
articles.summary: Tallinn’s decision to shut road border crossings comes after an attack on a drone manufacturer.
articles.body:
Moscow has accused Estonia of planning to build a “new Iron Curtain”, and promised to respond, after the small Baltic nation formally decided to close all border crossings with Russia to the east and south.

Estonia’s government on Friday approved a preliminary six-month closure of its road border crossings from December 1, and will decide next year whether to extend it.

Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova told a news briefing in Moscow that “should Tallinn proceed with these plans, our country will take the necessary political and diplomatic measures in response to safeguard its national interests.”

“Such moves are tantamount to attempts to erect a new Iron Curtain under the false pretence of some sort of threat from the East,” Zakharova added.

In Tallinn on Friday, Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna described the border closure as “an important measure”.

“It will reduce opportunities to exploit cross-border movement to recruit people, conduct influence operations, organise acts of sabotage or circumvent sanctions,” he said.

Estonia, a NATO and EU member and a staunch supporter of Ukraine, first announced the border closure earlier this month, accusing Russia of being behind an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

The Kremlin denied the accusation at the time, saying it was part of what it called a pattern of false allegations levelled against Moscow by European countries.

Estonia’s northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations ⁠Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.

Of the 760,000 people who crossed the Estonia-Russia border this year, 307,000 were Russian nationals, 175,000 were Estonian citizens and 54,000 held Finnish passports, Estonian ‌police ‌data showed.

Rail freight is not affected by the road closure, but remains subject to strict customs checks, Estonia said.

articles.title: A Canadian buyer found water rising through his basement floor two days after taking possession of a house; a judge ruled the seller had failed to disclose earlier water infiltration and awarded him C$129,595
articles.summary: A homeowner in North Bay, Ontario, has won judgment of CAD 129,595.75 against the seller of a house advertised as being in move-in condition.
articles.body: A homeowner in North Bay, Ontario, has won judgment of CAD 129,595.75 against the seller of a house advertised as being in move-in condition. According to the judgment in Austin v. MacFarlane, 2026 ONSC 463, Dale Austin bought the property from Lynn MacFarlane in May 2019. On 3 May, water came up through the basement flooring where a piano rested. A contractor later found significant mould and numerous foundation cracks. The judge found that water infiltration existed before May 2019 and that MacFarlane was, at best, wilfully blind or reckless as to it. Judgment was entered for negligent misrepresentation and general damages.What defects did the homeowner discover after buying the houseThe judgment records that Austin took possession on 1 May 2019. On 3 May, movers brought the piano into the basement rec room, and water came up through the flooring wherever the piano rested. According to the judgment, this was the first time Austin noticed any water issue, and he called his real estate agent straight away. He paid the movers C$800.00 to dig out the northwest corner of the house and fix a crack with a combination of tar, Blueskin, spray foam and silicone. Over the following days, he met contractor Josef Falk, who carried out an initial assessment of the property and the repairs required.The court heard that Falk, who specialised in basement repairs, first visited the property in May 2019. According to the judgment, he saw a large crack in the foundation on the north side, near the east corner, which extended into the ground and was wide enough near the top for his fingers to fit into. After removing drywall in the affected areas of the rec room and laundry room, he observed significant mould, water-damaged drywall and numerous cracks in the foundation. The judgment records that he also noted that a door or large window had been closed at some earlier time, and he believed that work was not done to code. He testified that the windows were pushed in significantly, which he concluded was due to the way the deck was built and attached to the house.Some of the drywall he removed carried manufacturer's date stamps from 2015 and 2017, and he found six or seven such pieces along the north wall of the rec room and laundry room. He also observed newer studs alongside older ones, drywall fixed with both screws and nails, two types of insulation, and a vapour barrier that had been cut and resealed with tuck tape.What did the engineer find in the home's foundationAccording to the judgment, structural engineer Eugene Longstreet, hired by Falk in May 2019, provided a report in December 2019. He observed vertical and horizontal cracks in the foundation, a place where the block wall was pushed in by approximately two inches, and a location where an old doorway appeared to have been filled in. The judgment states that he also saw that the hole left by a deck pier was three feet, six inches deep, and he testified that the minimum frost depth for construction in North Bay is four feet. The repair work ran from May to November 2019. It involved removing the deck, excavating the north side of the house, jacking the house, replacing cement blocks along the northeast and northwest sides, and demolishing the drywall, vapour barrier and insulation in the rec room and laundry room. Mould was found during construction, and a temporary exhaust hose was installed to remove bad air.The judgment records that Lynn MacFarlane testified that she bought the house in the fall of 2010 and lived there with her daughter until the end of April 2019. She denied having significant water infiltration in the basement and denied being aware of any cracks in the foundation. She told the court that in 2017 her father filled a hole she described as smaller than a dime in the crawl space and replaced a piece of drywall in the rec room, about 3 feet by 3 to 4 feet, to repair furniture damage. Her father, Dean MacFarlane, testified to repairing a pin-sized hole in the foundation at the front of the house and to cutting out a section of drywall about 3 feet high, plus a second piece about 16 inches square.According to the judgment, the judge found that the drywall repairs went beyond the small area the defendant acknowledged, relying on Falk's evidence about the dates on the drywall, the inconsistencies in the insulation and the studs. The judge found that water infiltration existed before May 2019, rejected the defendant's evidence that she had only touched up baseboards after her dog chewed them, and found that she was, at best, wilfully blind or reckless as to the water infiltration. The judge also found that Dean MacFarlane was mistaken or dishonest about the extent of his work.Why did the court award the buyer C$129,595On the representations, the judgment records that the MLS listing described the property as a "very well maintained home in a great neighbourhood", and also as economical to operate and in move-in condition. The MLS data entry form was initialled on each page by the defendant and signed and dated 4 January 2019. According to the judgment, the Warranties and Bill of Sale, signed on 30 April 2019, stated that no damage had occurred to the property since it was inspected by the purchaser and that the warranties would survive closing. Applying the five-part test for negligent misrepresentation from Queen v. Cognos, the court found a duty of care, an untrue, inaccurate or misleading representation, negligence, reasonable reliance and resulting damage. An intention to deceive is not required. The home inspection report was not relied on for the truth of its contents because Grasser did not testify, and the judgment states that latent defects are a limitation of a home inspection report.The court awarded the claimed repair costs of CAD 119,595.75. The judgment lists them as a receipt from Robert V. Smith for CAD 800.00, an application for a building permit for CAD 400.00, and Dale’s Construction invoices of CAD 30,000.00, CAD 25,000.00, CAD 56,728.75 and CAD 6,667.00. The judge found that Austin had met his duty to mitigate, noting that he acted quickly to stop the water infiltration from worsening, repaired only the damaged portions of the foundation, replaced the deck with standard materials and stayed in the house during construction to avoid relocation costs. Austin received CAD 15,594.88 from his insurer for interior basement repairs, but both parties agreed that the damage award is not reduced by that amount under the private insurance exception. Of the CAD 100,000 sought for loss of enjoyment, inconvenience and mental stress, the court awarded CAD 10,000, stating that there was no medical or other therapeutic evidence quantifying the effect on Austin and that damages could not be awarded for the impact on his mother because she was not a party to the action. The court awarded no punitive damages, finding that the case did not involve facts so abhorrent as to warrant such an award. Judgment was entered for CAD 129,595.75 for negligent misrepresentation and general damages, with prejudgment and post-judgment interest under the Courts of Justice Act. Austin was entitled to costs, and if the parties could not agree, written submissions limited to three typewritten pages were due from the plaintiff within 30 days and from the defendant within 14 days of receiving the plaintiff’s submissions. The judgment also notes that Austin had received CAD 10,000.00 in settlement from the home inspector, Brad Grasser.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani tore his Achilles tendon during a friendly soccer match against members of the City Hall press corps, with the 35-year-old saying he will have to wear a medical boot for six to eight weeks and could return to the pitch in about nine months.Mamdani arrived at a news conference on crutches on Friday and confirmed the injury when a reporter asked him about it. He said it happened during Thursday night's game and blamed his failure to warm up properly.“I did not stretch,” he said, as quoted by AP.The mayor, an avid soccer fan, also recalled scoring shortly after joining the match. “I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch, and I forgot that I was 35,” he said.Mamdani said he tore his Achilles soon after scoring and would be unable to play soccer for about nine months. He was also quick to point out that his team had beaten the journalists.The match was played at an indoor soccer facility in Manhattan's Financial District between members of the mayor's staff and around two dozen journalists. Mamdani arrived after the 7 pm kick-off and joined the game shortly after it began. The match was played seven-a-side on a small indoor pitch.The mayor's office claimed a 10-5 win, although accounts of the final score differed, with some journalists putting it at 8-4 or 8-5. Mamdani's injury occurred while he was chasing the ball and was not caused by contact with another player, according to local reports.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A former Platte County, Missouri, deputy treasurer says she was fired after reporting that her boss allegedly wrote a $1.3 million cheque from a county account to himself and told her to keep it in a safe; she is now suing
articles.summary: A former Platte County chief deputy treasurer is suing her former boss, the county treasurer, and the county, alleging she was fired after raising
articles.body: A former Platte County chief deputy treasurer is suing her former boss, the county treasurer, and the county, alleging she was fired after raising concerns about a $1.3 million transaction. Kimberlie Miller filed a lawsuit on Tuesday against the county and Treasurer Chris Kendall, according to a report by KCTV5. She alleges that she lost her job after reporting a $1.3 million cheque that she says Kendall wrote to himself. The lawsuit also accuses Kendall of discrimination, harassment, retaliation and wage violations. Kendall denied the allegation involving the cheque, saying it was made payable to the Platte County Treasurer, not to him personally.The cheque that raised concernsWhile Miller was working as chief deputy treasurer, her boss, Chris Kendall, allegedly emptied a county account at Central Bank by issuing a single cheque for its entire $1.3 million balance. According to the lawsuit, Kendall instructed her to “put it in the safe and ‘sit on it,’ but not discuss it with anyone” until he could arrange for the cheque to be deposited into a different, allegedly unapproved account at Weston Bank.Miller grew suspicious of these instructions and decided not to stay quiet. She reported the cheque to the county’s internal auditing department, the administrator for the commissioners and the county recorder. Kendall learned of the report and demanded a meeting with her, according to the court documents. Concerned that she would be punished, she asked to bring a witness. Miller claimed that Kendall would not wait and began yelling at her to come to his office immediately. She refused to meet without a witness. Miller says the county fired her on 12 December 2025 because of that refusal.The lawsuit lists six counts, including public employee whistleblower retaliation, sex discrimination, harassment, disability discrimination, age discrimination and retaliation for reporting discrimination. Miller also brings a state wage claim against both the county and Kendall. In the lawsuit, Miller alleges that Kendall often spoke about preferring younger workers. She says he questioned her medical history and threatened to interfere with her doctor's appointments. She also alleges that she did not receive the full pay rise she had been promised, that she was penalised for complaining about discrimination and that the county did not pay her overtime for hours worked beyond 40 in a week. She is seeking financial damages and a jury trial.Kendall has pushed back against the cheque allegation. In a statement to the television station, he said: “The allegation states that I emptied a Platte County bank account and issued a cheque to myself for approximately $1.3 million. That characterisation is categorically false. The transaction involved a certificate of deposit reaching maturity. The 3 December 2025 bank disbursement cheque, which is a matter of public record, was made payable to the Platte County Treasurer, not to me personally.”He added: “The funds remained County funds and were subsequently reinvested with another local financial institution. This was a County investment transaction, not a personal withdrawal or payment to me.” He said he would not comment on the other allegations while the case is pending. The case is set for a hearing on 19 February 2027 at 9 am in Platte City.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
